name: acral persistent papular mucinosis
aliases: acral persistent papular mucinosis (localised lichen myxoedematosus)

clinicalPearls: A distinct localised variant of lichen myxoedematosus confined to the dorsa of the hands and the extensor aspects of the distal forearms and wrists.
Presents as multiple small, firm, flesh-coloured to ivory-white papules that are persistent and usually asymptomatic.
Shows a strong female predominance and typically arises in middle adulthood.
Unlike scleromyxoedema, it is not associated with a paraprotein, thyroid dysfunction or systemic organ involvement.
Histology shows focal deposition of dermal mucin (mainly hyaluronic acid) in the upper reticular dermis without the fibroblast proliferation and fibrosis of scleromyxoedema.
The clinical course is benign and non-progressive, so reassurance rather than aggressive therapy is appropriate.
Careful distinction from generalised and sclerodermoid lichen myxoedematosus is essential because the latter carries systemic implications.
reference.pathophysiology: The condition results from a localised accumulation of dermal mucin, predominantly hyaluronic acid, produced by dermal fibroblasts and deposited in the upper reticular dermis of acral skin. In contrast to scleromyxoedema, there is little or no fibroblast proliferation, no significant fibrosis and no associated circulating paraprotein, and the process remains confined to the distal extremities. The underlying trigger for the localised glycosaminoglycan deposition is unknown.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with mucin stains such as Alcian blue or colloidal iron
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to exclude a paraprotein
Fasting glucose to exclude a secondary metabolic association
Clinical mapping of lesion distribution to confirm the acral, localised pattern
redFlags: Induration or sclerosis spreading proximally beyond the hands and forearms, suggesting scleromyxoedema
Development of systemic symptoms or organ involvement
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and persistent but non-progressive, with no systemic risk; lesions tend to remain stable over years.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the condition as scleromyxoedema and subjecting the patient to unnecessary systemic investigation and treatment.
Failing to recognise a truly generalised mucinosis with an underlying paraprotein that has been misclassified as the acral variant.
Interpreting focal dermal mucin without clinical correlation, missing the characteristic acral distribution.
references: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
